title: Mutual Fund Growth vs. IDCW: Understanding Returns & NAV
description: Growth plans reinvest all earnings, leading to an increase in the Net Asset Value (NAV) and compounding wealth over time. IDCW (Income Distribution cum Capita.

faq.a: IDCW stands for Income Distribution cum Capital Withdrawal. It is the current terminology used by SEBI for plans that distribute earnings to investors, replacing the older term 'dividend option' to clarify that payouts are not solely from dividends and can include capital appreciation.

No, IDCW payouts are not guaranteed. They depend on the fund's distributable surplus, which is influenced by its performance and market conditions. The frequency and amount of payouts are at the discretion of the Asset Management Company (AMC).

faq.q: Can I switch between Growth and IDCW options?
faq.a: Yes, you can typically switch between Growth and IDCW options within the same mutual fund scheme. However, such a switch is treated as a redemption from one option and a fresh purchase into another. This means it will trigger capital gains tax implications on the original investment.

IDCW payouts are fully taxable in the hands of the investor as 'Income from Other Sources' and are added to your total income, taxed at your applicable income tax slab rate. TDS of 10% is applicable if the payout exceeds ₹5,000 in a financial year.

faq.q: Does NAV alone indicate better performance?
faq.a: No, NAV alone does not indicate which option performs better. A Growth plan's NAV will generally be higher because earnings are reinvested, while an IDCW plan's NAV will be lower due to payouts. To compare performance, you must consider the total return, which includes both NAV appreciation and IDCW payouts.

faq.q: Is re-investing IDCW the same as a Growth plan?
faq.a: While you can opt to reinvest your IDCW payouts, it is not entirely the same as a Growth plan. Reinvesting IDCW involves receiving the payout (which is taxed) and then using that net amount to buy new units, whereas a Growth plan automatically reinvests earnings pre-tax, leveraging the full power of compounding.
